passage: Nitin sat on the flat's living room floor and piled up wooden blocks, one on another: one, two, three, four, five, six. At the sixth the tower toppled with a clatter. Farhan, Nitin's older cousin, looked up from his book. Nitin did not cry or complain, only said "Again," and built it once more, this time with the long block first and the small ones later. It grew to seven before it fell.

qa.q: How many blocks were in the tower when it fell the first time?
qa.a: The tower fell when the sixth block went on.

qa.q: What was Nitin feeling after the tower toppled?
qa.a: Nitin was calm and determined, since there was no crying and only "Again," and the rebuild started right away.

qa.q: What alternative approach could help Nitin build higher, and why?
qa.a: Nitin could ask Farhan how he would stack the blocks, or make the bottom wider, because a small change to the base can matter more than luck.

qa.q: How might Farhan see Nitin's way of building?
qa.a: Farhan sees a patient child trying a new order each time; he keeps reading instead of stepping in, which suggests he trusts Nitin to work it out.

grounding: A child stacks blocks into a tower, watches it fall at the sixth, and builds again with the blocks in a slightly different order.

passage:
"How tall, Vaibhav?" Vandana asked from the sewing machine.
"Up to the table!" He set down a blue block, then red, then another.
"Four... five..." she counted.
The sixth block went on and the whole tower tipped over.
"Oh no!"
Vaibhav didn't answer. He started again: red at the bottom this time, then blue.
"New order?"
"Just trying," he said.

qa.q: At which block did the tower tip over?
qa.a: It tipped over when the sixth block went on.

qa.q: What was Vaibhav feeling when the tower fell?
qa.a: He seemed calm and determined rather than upset, starting again without a word.

qa.q: What else could Vaibhav try besides changing the order?
qa.a: He could put the biggest blocks at the bottom on purpose, because a wide base is steadier than a random order.

qa.q: How does Vaibhav's rebuilding look to Vandana?
qa.a: Vandana finds it interesting and supportive to watch, asking about his new order and letting him get on with it.

grounding: A child's tower falls at the sixth block, and he simply rebuilds it with the blocks in a slightly different order.

passage:
Note for Yogesh's mother, Dilnaz
Today in free play Yogesh built a tower with the wooden blocks. It fell when he added the sixth block. He looked at the pile for a second, then built it again, but swapped the bottom two. It fell at six again. He tried a third order. I did not step in; he seemed happy to keep testing.

qa.q: What did Yogesh swap on his second try?
qa.a: He swapped the bottom two blocks.

qa.q: What was Yogesh feeling as he kept rebuilding?
qa.a: He seemed happy and curious, keen to keep testing rather than frustrated.

qa.q: What else could help Yogesh get past six blocks?
qa.a: Noticing which blocks make a wider base and putting them lowest, since changing the order at random may not fix the wobble.

qa.q: How might Dilnaz feel reading the note?
qa.a: Dilnaz would likely feel pleased that Yogesh is persistent and that the note-writer let him explore.

grounding: A teacher's note describes a child rebuilding a fallen tower in slightly different orders by trial and error.
